about: How scripts/review_questions.py shows the checklist of model.json to teachers. Each item is a flaw (a known item-writing or feedback problem, flagged with a quote and a suggested fix), a feature (described, not judged), or hidden (not shown: it needs other questions to judge, or its definition mixes a good and a bad case). The groups come from item-writing guidance, not from the signs of the fitted coefficients, several of which reward flaws.

items.label: Gives the constants or reference values needed
Requires a calculation
The stem includes details not needed to answer
items.why: Unneeded details make students spend effort on reading rather than on the concept, unless sorting relevant from irrelevant information is the goal.

items.label: Wrong options reflect common misconceptions or slips
Numbers or option patterns allow a shortcut
items.why: Students can reach the answer from the numbers or the layout of the options without the reasoning the question targets.

items.label: Feedback works through the steps
Uses formulas, symbols or codes
Asks for a name, date or naming convention
Asks for a definition or term without a scenario
Sets the question in a scenario
The stem says what kind of thinking is asked for
Describes a process or change over time
States where a process starts and ends
Can be answered from everyday experience alone
items.why: If common sense gives the answer, a correct response does not show that the student knows the science concept.

items.label: Options are full statements rather than single words or numbers
Uses a special format, such as evaluating someone's claim
Defines the system and its terms precisely
The correct option is longer or more detailed than the others
items.why: Students learn to pick the longest or most qualified option, so their scores rise without learning the concept.

items.label: All options have the same form and length
Each option gives a claim with a reason
Options give a definition next to each term
Each option combines two or more parts
Options cross two choices (for example, increases/decreases and because A/because B)
A wrong option can be ruled out without knowing the content
items.why: Options that contradict the stem or are obviously silly leave fewer real choices, so guessing gets easier.

items.label: Only wrong options use words like 'always', 'never', 'all' or 'only'
items.why: Students learn that extreme wording marks a wrong option and can answer without the concept.

items.label: Wrong options swap or reverse parts of the correct one
Wording in the stem points to the correct option
items.why: Students can match words between the stem and an option instead of reasoning about the question.

items.label: The stem sets two or more conditions the answer must meet
Shares content with other questions in the set
Feedback explains the principle behind a calculation
Feedback gives a rule or mechanism that carries over to other questions
Feedback states a general rule or warns about a common error
Feedback explains why, not only what
Feedback states a general law or definition
Feedback gives an everyday example or analogy
Feedback contrasts cases or maps the question to the rule
Feedback explains technical terms in plain words
Feedback goes beyond the question to wider principles
Feedback explains each part of a multi-part answer
Feedback traces a process step by step
Feedback mostly repeats the question or the answer
items.why: Feedback that restates the answer gives students nothing new to learn from when they get it wrong.

items.label: Feedback disagrees with the question or the options
items.why: A mismatch between the feedback and the question confuses students about which statement is right.

items.label: Feedback adds ideas beyond what the question needs
Feedback explains why wrong options are wrong
Contains a possible factual or scientific error
items.why: Students practise and remember the error. Check this one first.
